title: Evaluating Fish Screen Criteria for Juvenile Green Sturgeon
content:
ABSTRACT

Instream water diversions contribute to fish population declines through habitat loss and direct mortality, and this is a problem worldwide. Fish screens help prevent fish entrainment; however, in North America, screen protectiveness under current criteria developed from swimming physiology of salmonids remains unknown for many other affected species. Juvenile sturgeon likely encounter fish screens when migrating downstream. We experimentally evaluated the behavioral and physiological responses of juvenile Green Sturgeon (Acipenser medirostris) exposed to fish screen operational conditions to assess whether current salmonid criteria would also be protective for sturgeon. Experiments were conducted under different combinations of approach (perpendicular to screen) and sweeping (parallel to screen) water velocities across diel phases at two different fish size classes (6–10 cm and 16–21 cm fork length). Mortality, swimming behavior, and physiological stress responses were assessed to quantify lethal and sublethal impacts. No mortality and a limited number of screen impingement events were observed across all trials. Faster sweeping velocities (61 cm/s) reduced contact frequency with the screen but triggered elevated physiological stress responses in smaller juvenile sturgeon. Cortisol levels recovered within 24 h, whereas lactate and glucose responses persisted longer. Larger juveniles recovered more rapidly, indicating increased resilience with body size. Stress responses were also more pronounced during daytime exposures. These results suggest that a single encounter with diversion screens meeting current operational criteria may not cause acute mortality for juvenile Green Sturgeon larger than 6 cm, but smaller individuals are more sensitive to transient hydrodynamic stress. In natural river systems, repeated encounters with diversion infrastructure may produce cumulative physiological stress. Our findings provide empirical evidence to inform the evaluation and refinement of fish screen operational criteria and improve the ecological performance of diversion infrastructure for sturgeon and other fish species with limited swimming capacity.
